preamble: Raising of the near-open front vowel [æ] to open-mid [ɛ] is documented in Southern Hemisphere Englishes and in the history of German. In New Zealand English TRAP rose from [æ] to [ɛ] as the first step of the short front vowel chain shift (bad /bɛd/); South African English TRAP ranges from [æ] to [ɛ] (rabbit /ˈrɛbɨt/); and the Middle High German secondary-umlaut vowel ä [æ] was raised to [ɛ], so that ⟨ä⟩ is pronounced /ɛ/ in modern Standard German (mächtig, Wächter).

examples.note: In the short front vowel chain shift TRAP rose from near-open [æ] to open-mid [ɛ], while DRESS rose toward [e̝] and KIT centralized to [ə]; Cultivated NZE retains [æ].
Wiktionary gives [t̠ɹ̠̊˔æp] for General American and Australian English.
The from forms give the conservative [æ] pronunciation, still kept in Cultivated NZE.
TRAP ranges from [æ] to [ɛ] in General and Cultivated South African English; with KIT [ɨ], rabbit rhymes with abbot.
The from forms give the conservative [æ] pronunciation of TRAP.

examples.from: Middle High German mähtec, secondary-umlaut ä [æ] (Old High German mahtīg)
examples.note: The Middle High German near-open ä [æ] produced by secondary umlaut was raised to [ɛ]; Standard German ⟨ä⟩ is pronounced /ɛ/ (formerly /æ/).

examples.from: Middle High German wähter, wähtære, secondary-umlaut ä [æ] (Old High German wahtāri)
examples.note: Middle High German also had unumlauted wahter, wahtære.
